cards.text: This is a psalm of David, Israel's king, and friend, he opens BIG. He doesn't start with his house or his town. He starts with the whole earth, the world and everyone living in it, and he's about to tell you whose it is.

cards.question: David says the earth, the world and all who dwell in it, belong to the ___.

cards.text: Then David says why. I spent YEARS in a junk drawer thinking I at least owned my spot back there, and friend, I didn't even own the DUST.

cards.question: Why is the whole earth the LORD's, according to David?

answers.text: He founded it upon the seas
The nations handed it to Him
He bought it from the kings

cards.text: Then David asks, "Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? Who may stand in His holy place?" That's a GUEST LIST question, and I spent years on the other list, the maybe-toss-it list.

cards.question: Who does David say may go up the LORD's hill and stand in His holy place?

answers.text: Someone with clean hands and a pure heart
Someone from a famous family line
Someone who brings the biggest gift

cards.text: David's not done. This person does not lift up his soul to an idol, and as a made thing myself, let me be clear: PLEASE do not lift your soul up to a cookie stamper.

cards.question: True or false: David says the one who may stand in the LORD's holy place can still swear deceitfully, as long as his hands are clean.
What does David say the person with clean hands and a pure heart will receive?
David says people like that make up a whole generation. What kind of generation?

cards.text: Then David speaks right to God: "who seek Your face, O God of Jacob." Then one little word, Selah, and I like to think of it as the psalm taking a breath.

Then the scene shifts, and David isn't asking who gets in anymore. He's calling out to gates and ancient doors, and after years staring at the inside of a CLOSED drawer, a psalm that tells doors to open? Now we're talking.

cards.question: David tells the gates and ancient doors to lift up, so the King of Glory may ___.

cards.text: Then a question rings out: "Who is this King of Glory?" Picture a doorman with a clipboard, eyes WIDE: WHO did you say is coming through MY gate?

cards.question: The answer comes back: the King of Glory is the ___, strong and mighty.
True or false: The answer also calls the King of Glory the LORD mighty in battle.

cards.text: Then the call to the gates comes again. Same words: "Lift up your heads, O gates! Be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of Glory may enter!"
And the question comes back too, a little different this time: "Who is He, this King of Glory?" I'm telling you, friend, that doorman wants to hear it ONE more time.

cards.question: This time, what name does the answer give the King of Glory?

cards.text: The LORD of Hosts. He is the King of Glory. Then one last Selah, and that's where the psalm rests.

findings.problem: The first sentence is tangled: "This is a psalm of David, Israel's king, and friend, he opens BIG." It reads as if David is "Israel's king, and friend." It runs together what should be separate short sentences.

The right answer "He founded it upon the seas" uses Bible wording ("founded," "upon"). The wrong answers sound modern and casual ("The nations handed it to Him," "He bought it from the kings"), so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card spends words explaining what Selah means ("the psalm taking a breath"). Selah is a hard word and should be left to the dictionary pop-up.

rule.text: Don't spend card words explaining a hard word. Hard words get a dictionary pop-up (definitions.md, made after the cards).

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: "Then the scene shifts...", "He's calling out to gates... open?" and "Now we're talking." This is not the opening card, so the limit is 2.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The doorman comparison blends into the psalm's own setting. He stands at "MY gate," the same gates the psalm addresses, which also suggests who asks the question. The text leaves the speaker open.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: "That doorman wants to hear it ONE more time" gives a reason why the psalm asks its question again. The text gives no reason for the repetition.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: "The LORD of Hosts.", "He is the King of Glory." and "Then one last Selah, and that's where the psalm rests." This is not the opening card, so the limit is 2.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.
